Consider the following events;
$\mathrm{E}_{1}:$ Six fair dice are rolled and at least one die shows six.
$\mathrm{E}_{2}$ : Twelve fair dice are rolled and at least two dice show six.
Let $\mathrm{p}_{1}$ be the probability of $\mathrm{E}_{1}$ and $\mathrm{p}_{2}$ be the probability of $\mathrm{E}_{2}$. Which of the following is true?
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} \mathrm{p}_{1}=& 1-(\text { no die show six }) \\ & 1-\left(\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^{6}\right)=0.6651 \\ \mathrm{p}_{2}=& 1-(\text { no die shown two }+\text { one die shown two }) \\ \mathrm{p}_{2}=& 1-\left[\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^{12}+{ }^{12} \mathrm{C}_{1}\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^{11}\left(\frac{1}{6}\right)^{1}\right] \\=& 0.61866 \\ \mathrm{p}_{1}\gt & \mathrm{p}_{2} \end{aligned}$

questions.q: A box contains b blue balls and $\mathrm{r}$ red balls. A ball is drawn randomly from the box and is returned to the box with another ball of the same colour. The probability that the second ball drawn from the box is blue is -

questions.q: If a 3-digit number is randomly chosen, what is the probability that either the number itself or some permutation of the number (which is a 3 -digit number) is divisible by 4 and 5 ?
questions.solution:
We need 3 -digit number which is divisible by $4 \& 5$ both.
i.e. their last two digits are
$00,20,40,60 \& 80$
Now, ending with 00 are '9'.
$\{100,200, \ldots \ldots, 900\}$
If digit repeat other than ' 0 ' then they are
$\{220,440,660,880\}$
but 220 numbers can be permuted according to the condition as $\{220,202\}$
So, there are ' 8 ' other favorable cases.
If the number have no digit repeated like 320 .
320 can be permuted in 4 ways.
$\{302,230,320,203\}$
So, such numbers are $8 \times 4 \times 4=128$
Total favorable $=9+8+128=145$
So, required prob. $=\frac{145}{900}=\frac{29}{180}$

questions.q: A box contains coupons labeled $1,2,3$....n. A coupon is picked at random and the number $\mathrm{x}$ is noted. The coupon is put back into the box and a new coupon is picked at random. The new number is $y$. Then the probability that one of the numbers $\mathrm{x}$, y divides the other is (in the options below [r] denotes the largest integer less than or equal to $\mathrm{r}$ )
questions.solution:
Let $x=1$
favourable out comes $(1,1),(1,2) \ldots \ldots(1, n)$ no. of favourable out comes when $x=1$
=\left[\frac{\mathrm{n}}{1}\right]

$\therefore$ no. of favourable out comes when $x=1$ or $y=1$
=2\left[\frac{\mathrm{n}}{1}\right]-1

no. of favourable out comes when $x=2$ or $y=2$ but $x \neq 1, y \neq 1$
2\left[\frac{\mathrm{n}}{2}\right]-1

Similarly
no. of favourable out comes when $x=k$ or $y=k$ but $x, y \notin\{1,2, \ldots . . k-1\}$
2\left[\frac{\mathrm{n}}{\mathrm{k}}\right]-1

So probability $=\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left[\frac{n}{k}\right]-(1+1 \ldots . . n \text { times })}{n^{2}}$
=\frac{2}{\mathrm{n}^{2}} \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^{n}\left[\frac{\mathrm{n}}{\mathrm{k}}\right]-\frac{1}{\mathrm{n}}

questions.q: A purse contains 4 copper coins and 3 silver coins. A second purse contains 6 copper coins and 4 silver coins. A purse is chosen randomly and a coin is taken out of it. What is the probahility that it is a copper coin
questions.solution:
$\begin{array}{l}
\mathrm{P}_{1}: 4 \text { copper coins } \quad 3 \text { silver coins } \\
\mathrm{P}_{2}: 6 \text { copper coins } & 4 \text { silver coins } \\
\mathrm{E}=\text { Event of copper coin } \\
\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{E})=\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{P}_{1}\right) . \mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{E} / \mathrm{P}_{1}\right)+\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{P}_{2}\right) \cdot \mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{E} / \mathrm{P}_{2}\right) \\
=\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{4}{7}+\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{6}{10} \\
=\frac{41}{70}
\end{array}$

questions.q: A man tosses a coin 10 times, scoring 1 point for each head and 2 points for each tail. Let $\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{K})$ be the probability of scoring at least $\mathrm{K}$ points. The largest value of $\mathrm{K}$ such that $\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{K})\gt 1 / 2$ is $-$
questions.solution:
Ways to make the sum $K$ is coefficient of $x^{K}$ in $\left(x+x^{2}\right)^{10}$
Coefficient of $x^{K}$ in $x^{10}(1+x)^{10}$
Coefficient of $x^{K-10}$ in $(1+x)^{10}$
Which is ${ }^{10} \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{K}-10}$
So ways to make sum minimum $\mathrm{K}$ is
${ }^{10} \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{K}-10}+{ }^{10} \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{K}-9}+{ }^{10} \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{K}-8}+\ldots . .+{ }^{10} \mathrm{C}_{10}$
Probability
$\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{K}) &=\frac{{ }^{10} \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{K}-10}+{ }^{10} \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{K}-9}+\ldots \ldots \ldots \ldots . .+{ }^{10} \mathrm{C}_{10}}{2^{10}} \\
\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{K}) &=\frac{2^{10}-\left({ }^{10} \mathrm{C}_{0}+\ldots \ldots+{ }^{10} \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{K}-11}\right)}{2^{10}} \\
&=1-\frac{{ }^{10} \mathrm{C}_{0}+\ldots \ldots . .+{ }^{10} \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{K}-11}}{2^{10}}\gt \frac{1}{2}
\end{aligned}$
But $\mathrm{K}$ should be maximum so ${ }^{10} \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{K}-11}={ }^{10} \mathrm{C}_{5}$ (middle value) So that ${ }^{10} \mathrm{C}_{0}+\ldots .+{ }^{10} \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{K}-11}$ is $\max$ So $\mathrm{K}=16$
